spec.description:
Whether the cluster's nodes are keeping up with its pods, on any cloud.

Pods waiting for a node, how full each node pool is, what the autoscaler did about it, and whether the cloud could supply the node. Karpenter's own view on EKS is the Karpenter dashboard.

**Whether AKS's cluster autoscaler considers the cluster safe to scale, whether scale-down is paused, and nodes it would remove.**

**Nominal:** Safe to scale at 1, cooldown at 0 apart from the minutes after a scale-up, and a few unneeded nodes at most.

**Unhealthy:** Safe to scale at 0: too many nodes are not ready, and the autoscaler has stopped adding or removing any until they recover.
spec.title: Cluster Autoscaler State

defaults.noValue: Azure Monitor is pulled, but not for this cluster. Add it under pipeline.metrics.provider.azure.aks.clusters.

spec.description:
**Pods AKS's cluster autoscaler cannot place on any existing node, the worst of each five minutes.**

**Nominal:** Zero, or briefly non-zero while a node is added.

**Degraded:** Non-zero while the autoscaler is allowed to scale means it is not adding a node: the pool is at its maximum count, or Azure refused the VM for quota or capacity. The events on the Pending Pods tab carry its reason.

AKS runs the cluster autoscaler in its control plane, where nothing in the cluster can scrape it, so Azure Monitor is the only source of its metrics.
spec.title: Pods the Autoscaler Cannot Place

defaults.noValue: Azure Monitor is pulled, but not for this cluster. Add it under pipeline.metrics.provider.azure.aks.clusters.

spec.description:
**Node VMs Azure reports as unavailable, by scale set, at any point in each five minutes.**

**Nominal:** Zero.

**Unhealthy:** A VM down while Kubernetes still lists its node. Azure took it down for maintenance or a host fault, or its owner stopped it.
spec.title: Node VMs Down

defaults.noValue: Azure Monitor is pulled, but not for this cluster. Add it under pipeline.metrics.provider.azure.aks.clusters.

spec.description: Why this tab has no provider rows on it.
spec.title: No Provider Metrics

options.content:
**No cloud provider metrics are being collected.**

This is the default, not a fault. Pulling from CloudWatch, Cloud Monitoring or Azure Monitor is opt-in, because it needs a cloud identity with read access and every pull is billed.

- **EKS:** list the cluster under `pipeline.metrics.provider.cloudwatch.eks.clusters` for EC2 status checks, managed node group sizes and On-Demand vCPU usage. The gateway's role needs `cloudwatch:GetMetricData`, `cloudwatch:ListMetrics`, `tag:GetResources` and `autoscaling:DescribeAutoScalingGroups`.
- **GKE:** list the region under `pipeline.metrics.provider.gcp.compute.regions` for CPU and local SSD quota per machine family. `roles/monitoring.viewer` covers it.
- **AKS:** list the cluster under `pipeline.metrics.provider.azure.aks.clusters` for the managed cluster autoscaler's own gauges, which nothing else can read, and node VM availability. The identity needs Monitoring Reader on the cluster and its node resource group.

Without them, the other tabs still answer whether pods are waiting and what the autoscaler did; this one says whether the cloud was the reason.

spec.description:
**Each EKS managed node group's desired and in-service instances, against its maximum.**

**Nominal:** In-service equal to desired.

**Degraded:** Desired above in-service for longer than an instance takes to start: EC2 is not supplying the instances, for capacity or quota. Desired at the maximum is a group that cannot grow.

Karpenter's pools have no Auto Scaling group; the Karpenter dashboard covers them.
spec.title: Managed Node Groups

defaults.noValue: No managed node groups reported. Karpenter's nodes have none; if the cluster has some, add it under pipeline.metrics.provider.cloudwatch.eks.clusters.

spec.description:
**Cluster nodes failing an EC2 status check, by check.**

**Nominal:** Zero.

**Unhealthy:** **System** is the host under the node, which only AWS can repair; stop and start the instance to move it to another host, or let the autoscaler replace it. **Instance** is the node's own operating system, usually out of memory or disk. **Attached EBS** is a volume the node cannot reach.

From `pipeline.metrics.provider.cloudwatch.eks.clusters`, which finds the nodes by the cluster tag EKS and Karpenter set.
spec.title: Nodes Failing a Status Check

defaults.noValue: CloudWatch is pulled, but not for this cluster's nodes. Add the cluster under pipeline.metrics.provider.cloudwatch.eks.clusters.

spec.description:
**On-Demand vCPUs running in the region, for the whole AWS account.**

**Degraded:** Close to the account's quota for Running On-Demand Standard instances (Service Quotas code `L-1216C47A`), which CloudWatch does not publish. At the quota, every launch in these families fails, whatever the cluster's own limits allow.

Account-wide rather than the cluster's, because the quota is. Covers the standard families (A, C, D, H, I, M, R, T, Z), which include every instance type the Terraform examples use.
spec.title: On-Demand vCPUs in the Account

defaults.noValue: CloudWatch is pulled, but not for this cluster's nodes. Add the cluster under pipeline.metrics.provider.cloudwatch.eks.clusters.

**Nominal:** Well below 1.0.

spec.description:
**How much of the cluster's allocatable CPU and memory is promised to running pods through their requests.**

**Nominal:** Below about 0.85. An autoscaler keeps this high on purpose, removing nodes whose pods fit elsewhere, so a high reading with no pods waiting is efficiency rather than a problem.

**Degraded:** Near 1.0 with pods waiting for a node: the cluster is full and not growing. The Pending Pods and Cloud Capacity tabs say why.

**Requests, not usage**, the number the scheduler places pods by. Completed pods are excluded; pods still waiting for a node are too, since they are not on one yet.
spec.title: Requested Share of Allocatable

defaults.noValue: No metrics: kube-state-metrics is required

spec.description:
**Pods the scheduler has not placed on any node, because no node has room for them or satisfies their constraints.**

**Nominal:** Zero, or briefly non-zero while an autoscaler adds a node. These are exactly the pods an autoscaler acts on.

**Degraded:** Non-zero for longer than a node takes to start, a few minutes. Either the autoscaler is not adding a node, or the node it adds does not fit the pod. The Pending Pods tab says which.

Read from the pod's `PodScheduled` condition, which is false exactly while the scheduler has not found it a node.
spec.title: Pods Waiting for a Node

spec.description:
**What each autoscaler did about pods waiting for a node, newest first.**

Karpenter records `Nominated` when it has chosen a node for a pod, new or existing. The cluster autoscaler on GKE and AKS records `TriggeredScaleUp` when it adds a node for a pod, and `NotTriggerScaleUp` with the reason when no node group could take it: a group at its maximum size, or none whose nodes would fit the pod. `FailedScaleUp` is a scale-up the cloud refused, usually for quota or capacity; the Cloud Capacity tab says which.
spec.title: Autoscaler Decisions

defaults.noValue: No autoscaler decisions in this time range

spec.description:
**The scheduler's explanation for each pod it could not place, newest first.**

The message counts the nodes and the reason each was ruled out: `Insufficient memory` means no node has room, while `didn't match Pod's node affinity/selector` or `had untolerated taint` means no node of the right kind exists yet. An autoscaler adds a node for the first kind as long as a pool can hold the pod, and for the second only if a pool offers the kind asked for.
spec.title: Scheduling Failures
